title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 18)
summary: In part 18 of his Hagakure book club, NH covers impulsiveness, thinking 15 years ahead, strength of will, why failure and hardship are needed, and how ambition for rank must be controlled. He ties these back to lifting: long training timelines, failed squat attempts as preparation, and wanting everyone around him to be strong.
claims: NH says he tends to be impulsive in moments that require action, because acting removes the anxiety that inaction creates
Strike a middle ground between impulsiveness and procrastination: tolerate some anxiety so you can prepare and act precisely, but make the moment happen rather than waiting for it
Fixating on the finish line makes a task feel longer; losing yourself in the process, like simply running a race, makes time pass quickly
Believing 'your time will come' is an optimistic mindset that always pays off; if you believe it never will, it never will
Young people struggle to project themselves into the future because one year is a large share of their life; Hagakure asks you to think 15 years ahead
Decline of men happens in cycles of empires, not as a single global trend through time
NH wants everyone around him to be as great as him or greater; that is why he encourages people to lift rather than wanting to look big among skinny men
People who say 10 years of training is too long forget they will live those 10 years anyway
You must be true to yourself and keep promises to yourself before you can be true to others
NH has trained tens of thousands of hours, of which maybe 1% was seen by others; people judge you mainly by your words and the expression of your practice
Someone who has failed and got back up several times is better prepared for a crisis than someone who never failed
On the squat, a lifter who failed five times on the way to 300 lb handles a missed rep far better than one who never experienced failure
Failure is natural for anyone who tries things; the only problem is not getting back up
Modern society shields people from hardship for their first 25-30 years, producing entitled people who will be helpless if society collapses
The worst thing in a crisis is being taken by surprise; at least picture and think through hardship in advance
Material ambition must be present, since lacking that biological drive demoralises people, but it must be controlled or it possesses you
To change a system you must rise within it, but rising tends to corrupt you so you no longer want to change it
NH ranks the Hagakure books: book two is his favourite, book one second, book three least; Stoicism (Meditations first) starts in three weeks
